overview.title: 📖 Overview: Cataloguing the Eye's Blemishes
overview.subtitle: Bekhorot 38a–38b
overview.hebrewSource: הָרִיס שֶׁל עַיִן שֶׁנִּיקַּב, שֶׁנִּפְגַּם, שֶׁנִּסְדַּק, הֲרֵי בְּעֵינוֹ דַּק, תְּבַלּוּל, חִלָּזוֹן, נָחָשׁ, עָצָב
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: After closing out the technical measurement discussion for skull deficiencies (used earlier to calibrate the size of an ear-piercing), the Gemara moves to a new mishna cataloguing blemishes of the eye that permit a firstborn's slaughter: a torn or pierced eyelid, cataracts, and growths shaped like a snail, snake, or berry. The Gemara sorts out which cataracts count depending on whether they sit in the black or white of the eye, tells a story about a sage who ruled a halakha for his own benefit only because he had taught it beforehand, and defines exactly how long certain conditions — pale spots, constantly tearing eyes — must persist to count as permanent blemishes rather than passing ailments.

slides.title: 👁️ New Mishna: The Eye's Disqualifying Blemishes
slides.subtitle: Beyond blindness, several specific conditions of the eye permit slaughter
rows: The 'outer barrier' of the eye — Rav Pappa's definition
A film or cloudiness in the eye; counts depending on location (black/white) and whether sunken or floating
A thread of one color bisecting the iris and entering the other — disputed whether direction matters
A growth covering the pupil, considered a permanent blemish

callout.label: Terminology dilemma:
callout.text: Is 'snail-shaped growth' the same thing the Sages elsewhere call 'snake-shaped,' or are these two distinct blemishes? The Gemara resolves via a transmitted tradition that they are one and the same.

slides.title: ⚪⚫ Sunken vs. Floating: Two Contradictory Baraitot
slides.subtitle: A cataract's status depends on both its depth and its color

lines.speaker: Baraita 1
lines.text: A sunken cataract is a blemish; a floating one is not.

lines.speaker: Objection
lines.text: But another baraita teaches the exact opposite — sunken is NOT a blemish, floating IS!

lines.speaker: First try
lines.text: Perhaps one baraita discusses the black of the eye, the other the white — but 'there are no blemishes in the white'!

lines.speaker: Resolution
lines.text: Rabba bar bar Ḥana, citing Yoshiya of Usha: a black cataract — sunken is a blemish, floating is not; a white cataract — sunken is NOT a blemish, floating IS. Mnemonic: בַּרְקָא (white patches that float ARE a blemish).

callout.label: Result:
callout.text: Both baraitot are correct — each describes a different color of cataract, with opposite rules for sunken versus floating.

slides.title: 📖 Rabbi Shimon ben Yosei Lakonya's Lesson
slides.subtitle: Can a sage rule on a matter that benefits himself?

steps.content: 1️⃣ An elder, Rabbi Shimon ben Yosei Lakonya, calls a young Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Elazar to sit and teaches him: a snail-shaped growth in the eye is a permanent blemish permitting slaughter — and this is the same thing the Sages call 'snake'
2️⃣ He adds: though 'a person may not rule on blemishes for himself,' a teacher may instruct his students in halakha, and the students may then apply that ruling back to their teacher's own animal
3️⃣ Objection: doesn't Rav Huna say a scholar's self-interested ruling is heeded only if he stated it BEFORE the case became relevant to him?
4️⃣ Resolution: that is precisely what happened here — he had already been teaching this halakha to his students well before his own firstborn developed the blemish

callout.label: Principle:
callout.text: A ruling given in advance of self-interest, then applied by others, avoids the conflict-of-interest concern entirely.

slides.title: 🧵 The Tevallul Dispute: Which Direction Counts?
slides.subtitle: A thread of one color crossing into the other — Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yosei disagree

boxes.title: Rabbi Meir
items: Either direction is a blemish: white entering black, OR black entering white
Reasoning: tevallul means 'that which confuses (מְבַלְבֵּל) the eyes' — any mixing counts

boxes.title: Rabbi Yosei
items: Only white entering black counts as a blemish
Black entering white does NOT count, since 'there are no blemishes in the white of the eye'
Source: Psalms 73:7 calls the white 'the fat of the eye,' not 'their eyes' itself — so Leviticus 21:20's 'tevallul in his eye' excludes it

callout.label: The mishna follows:
callout.text: Rabbi Yosei's view — only a white thread entering the black pupil is called tevallul.

slides.title: 💧 How Long Must a Condition Persist?
slides.subtitle: New mishna: pale spots and constantly-tearing eyes, and the tests that confirm them are permanent
rows: Moist fodder, then dry fodder, with no improvement
Order matters — dry-then-moist does NOT prove the condition is permanent
Rain-watered fodder proves it; irrigated fodder does not
Only Rabbi Yehuda's version, per the Gemara's emended reading
Correlated to Adar–half-Nisan (moist season) and Elul–half-Tishrei (dry season)

callout.label: Rabbi Ḥananya ben Antigonus adds:
callout.text: For pale spots, examine the animal three separate times within the 80-day window to confirm the condition is truly constant.

summary.principle: The mishna catalogues specific, well-defined eye blemishes — eyelid damage, cataracts, tevallul, and growths — each governed by precise rules of location, color, and duration that separate a genuine permanent blemish from a passing ailment.

flowSteps.content: 👁️ Mishna lists eye blemishes: torn eyelid, cataract, tevallul, snail/snake/berry growths
⚪⚫ Cataract status depends on color (black/white) and depth (sunken/floating)
🧵 Tevallul: Rabbi Yosei rules only white-into-black counts, since 'no blemishes in the white'

columns.content: 📖 A sage may rule for his own benefit only if taught in advance
💧 Pale spots and tearing require set durations and fodder tests to confirm permanence

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: only precisely-defined, confirmed-permanent conditions of the eye qualify as blemishes permitting a firstborn's slaughter

quiz.q: According to the Gemara's resolution of two contradictory baraitot, when is a cataract (dak) considered a blemish?
o: Sunken cataracts are always a blemish regardless of color
A sunken BLACK cataract is a blemish and a floating one is not; a sunken WHITE cataract is not a blemish and a floating one is
Floating cataracts are never a blemish
Color makes no difference at all
quiz.e: The two baraitot are reconciled by color: for a black cataract, sunken is a blemish and floating is not; for a white cataract, the rule is reversed.

quiz.q: Why was Rabbi Shimon ben Yosei Lakonya permitted to rule that a snail-shaped growth was a blemish, even though it applied to his own firstborn?
o: Because a person may always rule on his own animal's blemishes
Because he had taught this halakha to his students before the matter became personally relevant, satisfying Rav Huna's condition for self-interested rulings
Because his students overruled him instead
Because snail-shaped growths are never disputed
quiz.e: Rav Huna's principle allows a scholar's ruling to stand even when it benefits him, provided he stated the halakha before the case arose — which Rabbi Shimon ben Yosei Lakonya had already done.

quiz.q: According to Rabbi Yosei, why does a black thread crossing into the white of the eye NOT count as a tevallul blemish?
o: Because tevallul only applies to eyelid damage
Because the white of the eye is called 'the fat of the eye' rather than 'the eye' itself, and 'there are no blemishes in the white'
Because Rabbi Meir already ruled it is not a blemish
Because black threads are always invisible
quiz.e: Rabbi Yosei derives from Psalms 73:7 that the white portion is termed 'fat,' not 'eye,' so Leviticus 21:20's phrase 'tevallul in his eye' excludes blemishes located in the white.

quiz.q: According to the mishna (following Rabbi Yehuda), how long must pale spots (chavarvar) persist to count as a permanent, disqualifying blemish?
o: 40 days
80 days
One year
Three days
quiz.e: The mishna follows Rabbi Yehuda's opinion that pale spots must persist for 80 days, as opposed to Rabbi Meir's baraita, which requires only 40 days.

quiz.q: In the fodder test for 'constant tears,' why does the order in which the animal is fed moist and dry fodder matter?
o: It doesn't matter at all
The animal must be fed moist fodder first and dry fodder afterward without improvement, to prove the tearing is a genuine permanent blemish rather than a temporary condition
Dry fodder must always be fed first
The animal must be fed only one type of fodder
quiz.e: The mishna specifies that only feeding moist fodder followed by dry fodder — with the eyes remaining unhealed — proves the condition is a true, permanent blemish.
